Do not add a trailing caveat after "but". - Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.
- Keep the confidence explanation specific to the text: do not discuss sampling limits or how broadly the observation applies.

Sample text:
---
The box was on the top shelf of the closet, behind a folded blanket and a jar of coins from countries that no longer existed. It was not a mysterious box. It was cardboard, soft at the corners, smelling faintly of dust and old rain. Inside were photographs with no names on the back. People standing in front of cars, people squinting into sun, a woman holding a cake as if it were a sleeping bird. I did not recognize any of them. For a long time I sat on the floor and tried to invent their lives, because a photograph without a story is a door with no house behind it.

One photograph showed a man in a pale suit standing beside a river. He held his hat in both hands, not as though he had just taken it off but as though he was offering it to the water. Behind him, a bridge crossed nothing I could identify. The sky was the color of cheap paper. I imagined he was waiting for someone who had promised to meet him at noon but had already decided, somewhere across the city, not to come. I imagined he knew this and stayed anyway, because waiting can be a kind of dignity. The photograph did not tell me whether he ever crossed the bridge. It only kept him there, suspended in the moment before leaving.

Another showed three children on a porch, arranged by height. The smallest held a stick like a scepter. The tallest had her hand on his shoulder, a gesture that might have been comfort or correction. They were all laughing at something outside the frame—someone behind the camera, perhaps, making a face. I liked this photograph because it had no tragedy in it. Not every old picture needs to become a ghost story. Sometimes a summer afternoon is just a summer afternoon, and the people in it are simply warm and alive and squinting against the light. The present is always disappearing, but it does not always leave a wound.

On the back of one photograph, in pencil almost rubbed away, someone had written: “After the storm, 1963.” The image itself showed a street covered in branches. A dog stood in the middle of the road, facing away from the camera, as if guarding the damage. The houses looked ordinary and stubborn. I wondered who had written the note, whether they had survived the storm, whether they were the kind of person who labeled things to keep from losing them. I am that kind of person. I write dates on folders and names on boxes. I believe memory is a shelf, and if I label everything correctly, nothing will fall.

But memory is not a shelf. It is a river with a habit of changing its bed. The photographs were proof: strangers preserved in moments that no longer belonged to anyone. Someone had kept them for decades, then forgotten them, then died, then left them to a house, then the house to me. I felt an odd responsibility. Not to identify them—I never would—but to acknowledge them. To look carefully. To say, silently: I see your hat, your cake, your dog in the road. I do not know your names, but you were here, and the light fell on you, and someone loved you enough to point a camera.

I put the photographs back in the box, but I did not return the box to the shelf. I left it on the table for a week. Every morning I passed it and thought, I should do something with that. Every evening I passed it again and thought, tomorrow. On the eighth day I opened it and chose one photograph—the man by the river—and slipped it into a book. I do not know why that one. Maybe because he looked like he was waiting, and I understand waiting. Maybe because the river was the only thing in the picture that was still moving, even after all those years, in the imagination of anyone who looked.

The book was a dictionary. I thought that was funny in a quiet way: an unnamed man hidden inside the definition of words, none of which could explain him. When I opened the dictionary weeks later, the photograph had shifted and was now marking the page for “threshold.” I decided not to move it. If a photograph can choose a word, who am I to argue? Threshold: the sill of a door; the entrance; the point of beginning. It seemed right for a man standing beside a river with his hat in his hands. Every crossing begins with someone standing still.

That night I dreamed of the box. It was full of keys, not photographs, and each key had a paper tag with a word on it: almost, afterward, home, enough, forgive. I tried one in a door that appeared in the middle of a field. The door opened onto the same field. I tried another key and it opened onto a kitchen I had never seen, where someone was making tea. I woke before I could thank them. The dream did not feel like a message. It felt like a mood, the way a house can feel like a mood. I lay in the dark and listened to the refrigerator hum.

In the morning, I labeled the box after all. On a scrap of paper I wrote: “Photographs, unknown, found in closet.” Then I crossed out “unknown” and wrote “unclaimed.” Then I crossed out “unclaimed” and left it blank. Some things do not want a name. They want only to be kept, the way a stone in a pocket is kept, not for its use but for the small weight of it. I put the box back on the shelf, behind the blanket, beside the jar of foreign coins. It is still there. Sometimes I think of the man by the river, still waiting in the dictionary at “threshold,” and I hope someone came. I hope the light changed. I hope he put his hat back on and walked.

Not every story needs to be solved. Some just need a witness, a quiet room, and a person willing to say: I remember you, even though I never knew you. That is enough. That is often enough.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: VARY

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A reflective, image-rich meditation turns a box of unidentified photographs into a story about memory, loss, and the value of witnessing.

## Grounded reading
The voice is gentle and attentive, with an elegiac mood that repeatedly makes room for ordinary happiness as well as loss. The narrator invents possible lives for strangers but resists claiming to know them; the emotional invitation is to look carefully, let uncertainty remain, and recognize that someone existed without needing to solve their story. The ending offers quiet reassurance rather than revelation: witnessing can be enough.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample foregrounds old photographs, labels and names, a man waiting beside a river, and the contrast between memory as orderly storage and memory as a changing river. It gives moral weight to acknowledging the unclaimed dead while also cautioning against turning every past image into tragedy. Its chosen resolution is modest: preserve the photograph, leave some names blank, and hope for the man by the river.

## Evidence line
> The present is always disappearing, but it does not always leave a wound.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the coherent return to images of keeping, naming, and witnessing makes the sample distinctive, though its lyrical reflection stays within a familiar elegiac mode.
